stem: A hazardous antineoplastic drug spills on a nursing unit. Which action should the nurse take?

options.A: Initiate the facility hazardous-drug spill procedure, obtain the designated spill kit and required PPE, and obtain trained assistance if required
options.B: Wipe up the drug immediately with routine unit cleaning supplies while wearing only standard examination gloves
options.C: Use a standard infectious-waste cleanup kit because hazardous-drug spills are managed the same way as biohazard spills
options.D: Leave the spill unattended until environmental services arrives, without initiating the hazardous-drug spill procedure

rationale: OSHA guidance states that healthcare settings where hazardous drugs are administered should have hazardous-drug spill kits available and that facilities should maintain spill-management SOPs. Workers involved in spill management should be trained; appropriate PPE is donned before cleanup, the spill kit is used to contain the spill, and trained help is obtained when needed. The spill size may determine who is authorized to perform cleanup. Routine supplies or an infectious-waste kit are not substitutes for the hazardous-drug procedure, and the area should not be left without initiating the facility response. Therefore A is the best answer.
educational_objective: Respond to a hazardous antineoplastic drug spill by following the facility hazardous-drug spill SOP, using the designated spill kit and appropriate PPE, and obtaining trained assistance when required.
source_organization: U.S. Department of Labor — Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)
source_document_title: Hazardous Drugs — Controlling Occupational Exposure to Hazardous Drugs
source_locator: Sections 'Spill Kits' and 'Clean-up of Spills': spill kits containing materials needed to clean hazardous-drug spills should be available; each facility should have SOPs for spill management; workers involved should be trained; spill size may determine who is authorized; general spill procedure includes assessing the spill, obtaining the spill kit, donning PPE, obtaining trained help if necessary, and containing the spill with the kit
source_claim_supported: Hazardous-drug spills should be managed under a facility spill SOP with a designated hazardous-drug spill kit, appropriate PPE, and trained personnel/assistance as required by the spill circumstances.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — Handling Hazardous and Infectious Materials, printed p.25 / PDF p.29: identify biohazardous, flammable and infectious materials; follow procedures for handling biohazardous and hazardous materials; demonstrate safe handling techniques
blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — Handling Hazardous and Infectious Materials / hazardous-drug spill response
correction_summary: Retained the hazardous-drug spill construct but removed the implication that every nurse should personally clean every spill regardless of training or spill size. Reframed the correct response around the facility SOP, designated hazardous-drug spill kit, appropriate PPE, and trained assistance when required. Replaced implausible distractors with realistic but unsafe alternatives.
audit_findings: A follows current OSHA hazardous-drug spill guidance and preserves the role/training nuance. B omits the designated spill kit and adequate PPE. C incorrectly treats hazardous-drug and infectious-material spill procedures as interchangeable. D fails to initiate the required response and leaves an exposure hazard uncontrolled. No spill-volume threshold or respirator requirement is universalized because those depend on spill characteristics. NCSBN 2026 explicitly maps hazardous-material handling to Safety and Infection Prevention and Control. Independent adversarial review found one best answer and no unresolved conflict.
audit_reviewer: GPT-5.6 Sol Rule 1 — item-by-item semantic audit
final_reaudit_scope: current OSHA hazardous-drug spill guidance; exact locator; claim-by-claim; A-D distractor audit; ambiguity/second-answer/cueing; NCSBN 2026 blueprint; independent adversarial second pass
